notes.b: Counselling is the first option for a couple in difficulty. It helps partners talk through their problems while there is still a chance to put things right, so that separation or divorce does not become necessary.
points: Counselling aims to help a couple resolve their problems before they become grounds for separation or divorce, which is why it is the first step rather than the last.
The service is confidential, so partners can speak openly. They may attend together, separately or, where relevant, with their children.
Several visits may be needed before the couple reach a resolution, because problems built up over time are rarely settled in one session.
The counsellor facilitates the discussion and may offer advice, but does not decide for the couple. The couple work out their own way forward.
Counsellors may refer a couple to a specialist counsellor for a particular problem, such as addiction or difficulties in sexual relations.
Marriage counselling is provided by Accord and by other independent counselling services in Ireland.
notes.tip: Counselling helps a couple decide whether to stay together, whereas mediation helps a couple who have already decided to part. Give two distinct points for counselling: it is confidential and it aims to resolve problems before separation or divorce, with the partners attending together or separately over several visits.

notes.b: Mediation is an alternative to court for a couple who have already decided to separate or divorce. Instead of a judge deciding the outcome, the couple work out the terms themselves with help.
points: The Family Mediation Service of the Legal Aid Board offers a confidential service to couples who have decided to separate or divorce. It was established in 1986, is State-funded and is free, whereas private mediators charge.
An impartial, trained mediator meets the couple together and helps them negotiate their own agreement. The mediator does not take sides or decide for them.
The issues negotiated include parenting arrangements, custody and access to children, finances and maintenance, and the family home and other property.
Mediation keeps children out of conflict, encourages communication between the partners, and helps them accept the separation.
Mediation is less costly, less adversarial and quicker than court proceedings, which pit the spouses against each other.
The outcome is a written agreement that each partner can bring to their solicitor to be made legally binding.
notes.tip: To explain how the Family Mediation Service helps, name an impartial mediator, say the couple negotiate their own agreement on custody, parenting, finances, home and property, and add that it improves communication, keeps children out of conflict and helps partners accept the separation. Do not describe mediation as counselling.

notes.b: Legal separation is a legally binding agreement under which spouses live apart but remain married. It lets a couple settle practical arrangements without going to court.
points: The spouses agree to live apart and set out the terms in a deed of separation, a legally binding written agreement.
Typical terms are living apart, care and access arrangements for the children, maintenance, and what happens to the family home.
A solicitor draws up the deed, and each spouse should have their own solicitor. A mediator may help them reach the terms.
Legal separation can be done without going to court if both spouses agree to the terms.
The spouses are still married, so neither can remarry. Only a divorce or a nullity decree allows that.
Where the spouses cannot agree, a court can grant a judicial separation. This is a court order, so it is different from a deed of separation, which the couple agree themselves.
notes.tip: Legal separation is not divorce: the spouses stay married and cannot remarry. In an evaluation, give a strength, such as the couple living apart with a binding deed on children, maintenance and the home, and a limit, such as being unable to remarry. Say who decides: the couple, through a deed drawn up by a solicitor.

notes.b: Nullity and annulment both declare that a marriage was never valid, but only a legal nullity decree has effect in the eyes of the State. Do not confuse either with divorce, which ends a marriage that was valid.
points: Legal nullity is a declaration by a court (the Circuit Court or High Court) that the marriage was never valid in law. The parties are then free to marry other people.
Couples married in a civil or State-recognised religious ceremony need a legal nullity decree before either spouse can remarry.
A marriage may be void, for example where one party is already married or in a civil partnership, the parties are within the prohibited degrees of relationship, or the formalities were not followed.

Nullity may also be granted for a lack of capacity or free consent, or where a marriage is voidable, for example because one spouse cannot sustain a normal marital relationship, including inability to consummate.
Church annulment is granted by a Church marriage tribunal, which studies the marriage and declares it invalid in the eyes of the Church.
A church annulment has no legal effect in the State, so the couple remain legally married. A civil nullity decree or a divorce is still needed before either can remarry civilly.
Nullity says the marriage never validly existed. Divorce ends a marriage that was valid.
notes.tip: The marks for church annulment versus legal nullity are for the difference in legal effect: a legal nullity decree from a court frees the parties to marry again, but a church annulment leaves them legally married.

notes.b: Divorce is a court decree that legally ends a valid marriage. It was introduced in Ireland by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, after the 1995 referendum.
points: The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 was amended by the Family Law Act 2019, which shortened the living-apart period from four of the previous five years to two of the previous three, and came into force on 1 December 2019.
First condition: the spouses must have lived apart for at least two of the previous three years. The couple can live apart under the same roof, and they do not have to be legally separated first.
Second condition: there must be no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, meaning no realistic chance of the spouses getting back together.
Third condition: proper provision has been or will be made for each spouse and for any dependent children, so that nobody is left without support.
The couple must also have a link to Ireland: either living here permanently, or one of them having lived here for at least one year before applying.

When granting a divorce, the court can make orders on custody and access, maintenance, the family home and other property, and succession rights, which extinguish a spouse's right to inherit from the other.
A decree of divorce is final, and each spouse is then free to remarry.
notes.tip: To outline the conditions for divorce, give three: living apart for two of the previous three years, no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision for the spouse and children. Use the current two-of-three-years rule. A divorce is decided by a court, not by the couple.

keyTerms.definition: A confidential service that helps couples resolve difficulties in their marriage before separation or divorce becomes necessary.
A confidential process in which an impartial mediator helps a separating couple negotiate their own agreement on children, finances and property.
A binding agreement, usually set out in a deed of separation, under which spouses live apart while remaining married.
A legally binding written contract between separating spouses that sets out the terms of their separation.
A court declaration that a marriage was never valid in law, which allows the parties to remarry.
A declaration by a Church marriage tribunal that a marriage is annulled, which has no legal effect in the State.
The legal ending of a valid marriage by a court, which allows each spouse to remarry.
The restoration of a normal marital relationship between spouses who have experienced difficulties.
A child who relies on a parent or guardian for financial support and care.

factCards.term: Three conditions for divorce under the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996
factCards.definition: The spouses have lived apart for at least two of the previous three years; there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation; and proper provision has been made for the spouse and dependent children.

factCards.term: Three areas a deed of separation covers
factCards.definition: The care of dependent children, maintenance, and arrangements for the family home.

factCards.term: Three things a family mediator does
factCards.definition: Meets the couple together as an impartial third party, helps them negotiate terms on children, finances and property, and encourages communication so that they can reach their own agreement.

factCards.term: Legal status of a church annulment
factCards.definition: It has no legal standing with the State, so the couple remain legally married.
Custody and access, allocation of property, payment of maintenance, and extinguishment of succession rights.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between legal separation and divorce, explaining whether the spouses remain married under each.
questions.model: Legal separation is a binding agreement, set out in a deed of separation, under which spouses live apart; the spouses remain married and cannot remarry. Divorce is a court process that legally ends a valid marriage, so each spouse is free to remarry once a decree has been granted. A legal separation can be arranged through mediation without court proceedings where both spouses agree; a divorce requires a court to be satisfied that the spouses have lived apart for the qualifying period, that there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and that proper provision has been made for the spouse and children.

questions.prompt: Outline the options available to a couple whose marriage is in difficulty, stating the purpose of each option and the conditions a couple must meet for divorce.
questions.model: Marriage counselling: a confidential service that helps couples resolve problems before they become grounds for separation or divorce; partners may attend together or separately, several visits may be needed, and specialist counsellors can be used for issues such as addiction. Family mediation: a confidential process in which an impartial mediator helps a separating couple negotiate their own agreement on parenting, custody and access, finances, maintenance and the family home, as an alternative to court. Legal separation: a binding deed of separation, drawn up by a solicitor, covering living apart, children, maintenance and the family home; the spouses remain married. Legal nullity: a court declaration that the marriage was never valid, which allows remarriage; a church annulment has no legal standing. Divorce: the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, as amended by the Family Law Act 2019, requires that the spouses have lived apart for the qualifying period set by the Act, that there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and that proper provision has been made for the spouse and dependent children; the court may then make orders on custody, property, maintenance and succession rights, and the decree cannot be reversed.
